title: I don’t know how to code, but I built a stock market website with AI — would love your feedback
author: Fast_Pilot304
selftext:
I’m interested in the stock market, but I don’t know how to code.  
I had an idea for a website I wanted to use myself, so I built it mostly through vibe coding with AI.  
The site is [ttbbtb.com](http://ttbbtb.com/). It organizes historical market drawdowns, all-time highs, recoveries, and market cycles so you can quickly see what happened in the past without digging through a lot of news.  
Since I’m not a developer, I’d really appreciate feedback from both developers and regular users.  
When you first visit the site:  
Is it clear what the site does?  
Is the information easy to understand?  
Is anything confusing or unnecessary?  
What would make you stay longer or come back?  
Would you actually find something like this useful?  
I’m still improving it, so honest criticism is very welcome.  
[https://ttbbtb.com](https://ttbbtb.com/)

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
Opened it cold without reading your post first. What the site does is clear within a few seconds, the drawdown table explains itself, so that part is working.

What I would fix is that every number is presented as settled fact with no source line. For historical drawdowns people will want to know which index, whether it is total return or price only, and where the series came from. Without that a sceptical visitor has no way to check you, and this is an audience that checks.

replies.author: Fast_Pilot304
replies.body: Thanks, really good point. I appreciate the feedback. I’ll fix this right away and make the data source and methodology much clearer.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: One line under each table is enough, series name and where it came from. The people who would bounce without it are the ones who would actually use the site.

replies.author: Fast_Pilot304
replies.body:
I’m using Finazon’s paid API for daily OHLC data.  
I found some errors in the historical data, so I’ve been filtering those out myself. I also emailed them several times about it, but haven’t received a reply.  
I chose Finazon because it was the cheapest option I could find for what I needed, but I’m now looking at other providers. If there are data issues and support doesn’t respond, I’m not sure the lower price is worth it.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: filtering by hand is fine as long as you write down the rule you filtered with. a bad print you deleted is a decision about the data, and six months on you will want to know which ones went. worth keeping a second source for a handful of names just to diff against, even a free one. did the errors cluster in particular tickers or dates?

replies.author: Fast_Pilot304
replies.body:
I wasn’t removing data based on a fixed rule. I was only deleting records that were obviously wrong — for example, non-trading days where OHLC were all 0, stocks that normally traded above $200 suddenly showing prices below $1, or cases where the daily high suddenly jumped above $20,000.  
The first time I noticed the issue, a large number of tickers were returning strange values on the same two dates, so at first I thought the problem was limited to those dates. But after looking into it more, I realized that similar bad values were also appearing sporadically across different tickers and dates, without any obvious pattern. They also weren’t occurring on stock split or reverse split dates.  
My calculations rely heavily on daily highs and lows, so even a single bad data point like that can significantly distort the results.  
The bigger issue is that I only removed the errors I happened to notice. There are probably still more bad records in the dataset that I haven’t found yet, and realistically I can’t check every record one by one.  
So I’m currently trying to figure out a better way to detect and validate these kinds of errors.  
Thanks for the advice — I really appreciate it.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: those are the ones I'd delete too. keep the list of what went, the rule can come later.

comments.author: Ok-Proposal6598
comments.body:
Para ser hecho sin programar, está bien resuelto. Probé bastante (código, la API que usa, seguridad, y la búsqueda de tickers escribiendo distintos símbolos) y no encontré nada roto ni nada sensible expuesto, lo cual ya dice bastante sobre cómo lo armaste.
Sobre tus preguntas: sí se entiende qué hace el sitio, el tagline y la descripción de arriba dejan claro el propósito. El "CURRENT READ" en texto plano ayuda mucho a traducir los números, buen detalle.
Donde sí le veo algo de fricción es en la densidad de datos: "reached this range 265 times, 235 formaron un low final" son números correctos pero para alguien sin trasfondo estadístico puede sentirse denso al primer vistazo. Un tooltip corto tipo "esto significa que X de Y veces el mercado se recuperó sin caer más" ayudaría a que no tengan que descifrarlo solos.
Para que alguien vuelva, yo agregaría algo tipo alerta o watchlist (que te avise cuando un ticker entra en una zona de drawdown que te interesa) o comparar dos tickers lado a lado. Ahora mismo es una herramienta de consulta puntual, no algo que dé ganas de revisar todos los días.
Sí lo encuentro útil, la combinación de drawdown + tiempo de recuperación + contexto de tasas de la Fed en un solo lugar no es algo que se vea tan seguido armado así de limpio.

replies.author: Fast_Pilot304
replies.body: Thanks, this is really helpful. I agree the stats could be easier to understand at a glance, so I’ll work on simplifying the wording and adding clearer explanations.
